name: Ascension morph (surgery preview morph)

lead: An ascension morph is an edited photo of a person's face showing how it could look if a set of changes were made, such as a leaner face, a more angular jaw and chin, lifted outer eye corners or a refined nose tip. The payoff is a visual target: people can see which changes would matter most before committing to any procedure.

On looksmax.org, morphs are often posted alongside a facial evaluation that lists objectives in order of importance and a projected rating after the changes. Practitioners say the images help prioritise; no published study has examined how well community morphs match surgical outcomes.

paras: A member posts photos and asks for a facial evaluation. An editor, often another member, retouches the image and lists the planned changes in priority order, sometimes with an estimated tier before and after. The result is discussed in the thread and used as a reference when planning procedures or non-surgical changes.

A morph is a manipulated image and does not account for tissue, bone structure or healing, so real outcomes can differ from the picture. Clinicians who use computer imaging in consultations generally describe it as an illustration rather than a guarantee. Heavy focus on edited images can also feed dissatisfaction with one's own face for some people.

angle.text: The morph does not change the face itself. It gives a concrete picture of a goal so a person can rank which changes (jaw, chin, eyes, nose, skin, weight) to pursue first and discuss them with others.

lead: An ascension morph (also called a predicted ascension morph or surgery preview morph) is an edited photograph that shows how a person's face might look after a list of aesthetic changes. In looksmaxxing communities, "ascension" means a major improvement in looks, and the morph serves as a visual plan for it.[1]

A typical thread on looksmax.org pairs a facial evaluation with a morph. In one example, the editor lists eleven objectives in order of importance, from a leaner face and greater angularity of the jaw, chin and cheekbones to lip proportions, outer eye corner lift, nose tip shape, eye colour, lashes, nasolabial folds and neck width, and states the intended rating change as "+2 tiers".[1] Other members ask whether the editor makes these for anyone or for payment, showing that morphing is also offered as a service.[1]
infobox: Objectives list, edited image, projected tier

paras: Morphs are made by editing a front or profile photo with retouching or liquify-style tools. The accompanying text usually names each intended change and ranks them by importance.[1]
The projected result is expressed in community rating terms, for example moving from a "high mtn" to a "low CL" tier.[1] These tiers are informal community labels rather than clinical measures.

Members request morphs together with facial evaluations and reply with reactions, questions about who made them and whether they were paid.[1] Proponents value them as a way to visualise a goal; they are generally discussed as previews, not promises.

Plastic surgery and orthodontic practices commonly use digital imaging in consultations to illustrate possible results. Such tools are described by clinics as communication aids, and the community morph is the informal counterpart made by peers.
No studies found. Research on clinic-based digital imaging in aesthetic consultations exists as a broader category but has not examined community-made ascension morphs.

lore.intro: Morphs are posted in evaluation threads as a standard part of the "facial eval" format.[1]

claims.claim: A morph shows the realistic result of the listed changes.
